children: The Australian dollar edged higher on Wednesday after a surprisingly hot reading on monthly inflation tempered market wagers on rate cuts for next year, while keeping alive the risk that further tightening might be needed.
, having bounced 0.2% overnight and away from an 11-month trough at $0.6597. Resistance stands at $0.6660, while a break of $0.6592 would risk a further retreat towards $0.6422.
The kiwi dollar was flat at $0.5477
, after bouncing 0.6% overnight. The currency is deeply oversold having hit its lowest since 2009 on Monday at $0.5434, but needs to get back above $0.5630 to stabilise.

Data showed consumer prices rose 0.5% in October and 4.9% for the year, led by monthly gains in fuel and clothing. The trimmed mean measure of core inflation also rose 0.5%, well above the 0.3% forecast and lifting the annual pace to 3.8%.
That was even further above the Reserve Bank of Australia's target range of 2% to 3% and showed why interest rates have already been raised five times this year to 4.85%.
The central bank had expected a high consumer price reading this quarter given the pulse from petrol prices, but not the outsized increase in core inflation.
"The renewed surge in underlying inflation will make for uncomfortable reading at the RBA," said Abhijit Surya, a senior APAC economist at Capital Economics.

"We're sticking with our view that the sharp deterioration in the labour market in recent weeks will be enough to dissuade the bank from hiking further, but the monetary policy outlook remains far from clear-cut."
Figures out last week showed unemployment spiked to 4.9% in October, well above analyst and RBA forecasts, stoking speculation about the next move in rates being down.
The inflation data led markets to scale back the chance of an easing by as early as May to 36% from 60%, while June edged down to 76%. (0#AUDIRPR)
"Rising inflation and unemployment are the RBA's worst nightmare," said Harry Murphy Cruise, head of economic research for Oxford Economics Australia.

"We maintain our view that rates will remain on hold at 4.85% through 2027 as the RBA prioritises its fight against inflation," he said. "But that risks unemployment breaching the RBA's 5.1% peak forecast."
